text: Welcome. This is the AIonOS servicing agent, running on a typical CTM servicing desk. Over the next few minutes, we'll follow one everyday problem, an airline schedule change, from the moment it lands in the inbox to a reissued ticket. With a consultant in control at every decision.
It's early on Thursday morning, and the shared servicing inbox has filled up overnight. Before a consultant opens a single email, the agent has already read every one of them.

Each message is classified by intent. Schedule changes. Exchanges. A refund enquiry. A virtual card decline from a hotel. And a handful that need no action at all: newsletters, auto-replies, and confirmations.

Non-actionable mail is filtered out, and a duplicate airline notification is merged into the traveller's own request. What remains is ranked by urgency, using departure time, traveller profile, and risk to the trip. Twelve emails become seven cases, and the most urgent one is at the top.
Let's open it. Sarah Chen, a finance director at one of CTM's corporate clients, has been moved by Qantas onto tomorrow's flight. She has a nine a.m. meeting in Singapore that she will now miss.

The agent retrieves her booking from Amadeus and reads the schedule change. Her flight this morning has been cancelled, and the airline's automatic re-protection lands her in Singapore eight hours after her meeting begins.

Next, the fare rules. Because the airline made the change, this is an involuntary change. The agent finds the Qantas waiver, confirms that change fees don't apply, and checks which partner airlines the ticket can be endorsed to.
Then, the client's travel policy. Qantas is the preferred carrier. Business class is allowed on flights over six hours. And any extra cost above five hundred dollars needs a manager's approval.

With all of that in hand, the agent searches for alternatives, and ranks three options that still get Sarah to Singapore tonight. Each one shows the arrival time, the cost, its policy status, and the reason for its ranking.
This is where the consultant steps in. Instead of twenty-odd minutes of reading, searching, and calculating, they review one clear recommendation, with the reasoning laid out. One click, to approve.
The agent then does the work. It cancels the old segment, books the new flight, reissues the ticket under the airline waiver, updates the booking record, and flags the change for invoicing.
It also drafts a reply to Sarah, in plain language, with her new flight and seat, ready to send by email or WhatsApp.

Every step is recorded in UniStack. Each action carries a timestamp, the data it used, the model behind the decision, its confidence, and its cost. The consultant's approval is captured, and the whole change can be rolled back with one click. This is how CTM can show that every automated action is transparent, explainable, and reversible.

The result. A case that typically takes a consultant around twenty-five minutes is resolved in under four, with a single human decision. And this isn't new for us. Our ticket reissue automation on Amadeus delivers more than ninety-three percent recommendation accuracy, with twenty-two percent faster resolutions.
So, pick the one flow that matters most to CTM, and we'll prove it on your own data in six to eight weeks, with no commercial commitment. Thank you.
